papers.abstract: Mathematical reasoning in large language models (LMs) has garnered significant attention in recent work, but there is a limited understanding of how these models process and store information related to arithmetic tasks within their architecture. In order to improve our understanding of this aspect of language models, we present a mechanistic interpretation of Transformer-based LMs on arithmetic questions using a causal mediation analysis framework. By intervening on the activations of specific model components and measuring the resulting changes in predicted probabilities, we identify the subset of parameters responsible for specific predictions. This provides insights into how information related to arithmetic is processed by LMs. Our experimental results indicate that LMs process the input by transmitting the information relevant to the query from mid-sequence early layers to the final token using the attention mechanism. Then, this information is processed by a set of MLP modules, which generate result-related information that is incorporated into the residual stream. To assess the specificity of the observed activation dynamics, we compare the effects of different model components on arithmetic queries with other tasks, including number retrieval from prompts and factual knowledge questions.

papers.title: Too Late to Recall: Explaining the Two-Hop Problem in Multimodal Knowledge Retrieval
papers.research_question: Why do many vision language models (VLMs) exhibit reduced factual recall performance compared to their large language model (LLM) backbones, and what is the underlying mechanism?
papers.core_contribution: VLMs suffer from a 'two-hop problem' where entity representations from visual inputs emerge too late in the forward pass, bypassing the early-layer MLP circuits in the LLM backbone responsible for factual recall, leading to performance degradation.
papers.conclusion: The speed of early entity resolution critically determines how effective VLMs are in using preexisting LLM mechanisms; representation misalignment limits VLMs' ability to reuse existing task circuits.
papers.key_findings:
11 out of 14 benchmarked VLMs exhibit factual recall degradation compared to their LLM backbones.
Attribution patching shows degraded VLMs do not use the same early-layer MLPs as their LLM backbones for factual recall.
Activation patching of early-layer MLP outputs from the LLM into the VLM recovers performance, indicating these components are causally crucial.
Linear probing reveals entity representations emerge in middle-to-late layers in degraded VLMs, but early in high-performing VLMs.
Chain-of-thought prompting can mitigate the performance gap for some VLMs, especially larger ones.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on factual recall and may not generalize to other tasks.
future_direction: Investigate better, more data-efficient adapter mechanisms and multimodal alignment techniques.
Examine other tasks beyond factual recall, comparing VLMs against their LLM backbone.
papers.abstract: Training vision language models (VLMs) aims to align visual representations from a vision encoder with the textual representations of a pretrained large language model (LLM). However, many VLMs exhibit reduced factual recall performance compared to their LLM backbones, raising the question of how effective multimodal fine-tuning is at extending existing mechanisms within the LLM to visual inputs. We argue that factual recall based on visual inputs requires VLMs to solve a two-hop problem: (1) forming entity representations from visual inputs, and (2) recalling associated factual knowledge based on these entity representations. By benchmarking 14 VLMs with various architectures (LLaVA, Native, Cross-Attention), sizes (7B-124B parameters), and training setups on factual recall tasks against their original LLM backbone models, we find that 11 of 14 models exhibit factual recall degradation. We select three models with high and two models with low performance degradation, and use attribution patching, activation patching, and probing to show that degraded VLMs struggle to use the existing factual recall circuit of their LLM backbone, because they resolve the first hop too late in the computation. In contrast, high-performing VLMs resolve entity representations early enough to reuse the existing factual recall mechanism. Finally, we demonstrate two methods to recover performance: patching entity representations from the LLM backbone into the VLM, and prompting with chain-of-thought reasoning. Our results highlight that the speed of early entity resolution critically determines how effective VLMs are in using preexisting LLM mechanisms. More broadly, our work illustrates how mechanistic analysis can explain and unveil systematic failures in multimodal alignment.

papers.title: Latent Chain-of-Thought? Decoding the Depth-Recurrent Transformer
papers.research_question: Does Huginn exhibit signs of latent chain-of-thought reasoning during inference?
papers.core_contribution: We find limited evidence of interpretable latent chain-of-thought reasoning in the depth-recurrent transformer Huginn-3.5B, and uncover significant probing inconsistencies across recurrent blocks.
papers.conclusion: We find little evidence of structured latent chain-of-thought reasoning in Huginn, but it may be more subtle or distributed than our tools can detect.
papers.key_findings:
Probing inconsistencies across blocks in Huginn's depth-recurrent architecture: hidden state interpretability depends heavily on block index and decoding method.
Token rank trajectory analysis provides little evidence for latent CoT reasoning.
Scaling recurrence depth fails to match explicit reasoning: increasing recurrent steps only marginally improves performance and falls short of explicit CoT prompting.
papers.limitation: The results do not definitively rule out the presence of latent CoT; it may be more subtle or distributed than our employed tools can detect.
future_direction: Apply more advanced probing techniques, such as activation patching, to uncover finer-grained reasoning patterns.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has enabled transformer-based language models to excel at complex mathematics and multi-step planning. However, in standard decoder-only architectures, these reasoning steps are externalized in natural language, improving interpretability at the cost of efficiency. To capture reasoning that is not easily represented in words, many works have explored recurrent architectures that aim to internalize reasoning in latent space, potentially supporting latent CoT. In this paper, we investigate whether such reasoning structures emerge in Huginn-3.5B, a depth-recurrent Transformer that reuses layers at inference time without increasing parameter count. We examine the model's internal behavior on arithmetic tasks using a suite of probing techniques including the Logit Lens and Coda Lens. Our findings reveal limited evidence of interpretable latent CoT by tracking rank trajectories of final and intermediate result tokens. Furthermore, we uncover significant probing inconsistencies across recurrent blocks, where the interpretability of hidden states depends heavily on both the layer index and the decoding method. Finally, we empirically show that increasing recurrence depth yields only marginal gains and falls well short of models that explicitly externalize reasoning steps. The code is available at https://github.com/wenquanlu/huginn-latent-cot.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Thinking Fast and Slow in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models exhibit human-like intuitive reasoning errors, and how do more advanced models avoid these errors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs exhibit human-like intuitive errors (System 1), but more advanced models (ChatGPT, GPT-4) avoid these errors through chain-of-thought reasoning and well-developed intuition, performing hyperrationally.
papers.conclusion: Psychological methods can reveal emergent traits in LLMs; advanced LLMs show remarkable reasoning abilities and can avoid intuitive errors, resembling both System 1 and System 2 processes.
papers.key_findings:
Early/smaller LLMs (up to GPT-3-curie) often give atypical responses, indicating poor task comprehension.
Larger pre-ChatGPT models (GPT-3-davinci family) show a high tendency to give intuitive but incorrect responses, similar to human System 1 errors.
ChatGPT models (especially GPT-4) show a high fraction of correct responses, often using chain-of-thought reasoning.
Instructing GPT-3-davinci-003 to use chain-of-thought reasoning reduces intuitive errors and increases correct responses.
Providing training examples (few-shot) improves GPT-3-davinci-003's performance on both CRT and semantic illusions.
papers.limitation:
The study only tested one family of LLMs (the GPT family).
The tasks used are limited in scope (CRT and semantic illusions).
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LLMs is not truly deliberate System 2 reasoning but resembles it.
papers.abstract: We design a battery of semantic illusions and cognitive reflection tests, aimed to elicit intuitive yet erroneous responses. We administer these tasks, traditionally used to study reasoning and decision-making in humans, to OpenAI's generative pre-trained transformer model family. The results show that as the models expand in size and linguistic proficiency they increasingly display human-like intuitive system 1 thinking and associated cognitive errors. This pattern shifts notably with the introduction of ChatGPT models, which tend to respond correctly, avoiding the traps embedded in the tasks. Both ChatGPT-3.5 and 4 utilize the input-output context window to engage in chain-of-thought reasoning, reminiscent of how people use notepads to support their system 2 thinking. Yet, they remain accurate even when prevented from engaging in chain-of-thought reasoning, indicating that their system-1-like next-word generation processes are more accurate than those of older models. Our findings highlight the value of applying psychological methodologies to study large language models, as this can uncover previously undetected emergent characteristics.

papers.title: Demystifying Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: What are the key factors that enable models to generate long chain-of-thought trajectories, and how can training strategies be optimized to enhance long CoT reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically investigates the mechanics of long chain-of-thought reasoning, identifying key factors such as reward shaping and verifiable signals, and provides practical guidance for optimizing training strategies to enhance long CoT reasoning in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The study provides practical guidance for optimizing training strategies to enhance long CoT reasoning, emphasizing the importance of reward shaping, verifiable signals, and careful design choices.
papers.key_findings:
SFT with long CoT scales to a higher performance upper limit than short CoT and facilitates further RL improvement.
Reasoning capabilities emerge with increased training compute, but reward shaping is crucial for stabilizing CoT length growth.
Scaling verifiable reward signals is critical for RL, and noisy web-extracted solutions with filtering show promise for out-of-distribution tasks.
Core abilities like error correction are inherently present in base models, but effective incentivization via RL demands significant compute.
The introduced Cosine Reward with repetition penalty can stabilize CoT length scaling and improve accuracy.
papers.limitation:
RL infrastructure is still in its infancy, with challenges in scaling to larger models due to hardware limitations and low utilization.
Smaller models may struggle to develop high-level reasoning skills and instead rely on heuristic-based pattern recognition.
Designing rule-based verifiers and curating prompt sets across different domains remains labor-intensive.
future_direction: Investigate RL using a larger base model.
Advancements in machine learning and systems research to overcome hardware limitations and accelerate progress in long CoT modeling.
Future research on silver supervision signals and self-supervised approaches in RL verification.
papers.abstract: Scaling inference compute enhances reasoning in large language models (LLMs), with long chains-of-thought (CoTs) enabling strategies like backtracking and error correction. Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial method for developing these capabilities, yet the conditions under which long CoTs emerge remain unclear, and RL training requires careful design choices. In this study, we systematically investigate the mechanics of long CoT reasoning, identifying the key factors that enable models to generate long CoT trajectories. Through extensive supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and RL experiments, we present four main findings: (1) While SFT is not strictly necessary, it simplifies training and improves efficiency; (2) Reasoning capabilities tend to emerge with increased training compute, but their development is not guaranteed, making reward shaping crucial for stabilizing CoT length growth; (3) Scaling verifiable reward signals is critical for RL. We find that leveraging noisy, web-extracted solutions with filtering mechanisms shows strong potential, particularly for out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks such as STEM reasoning; and (4) Core abilities like error correction are inherently present in base models, but incentivizing these skills effectively for complex tasks via RL demands significant compute, and measuring their emergence requires a nuanced approach. These insights provide practical guidance for optimizing training strategies to enhance long CoT reasoning in LLMs. Our code is available at: https://github.com/eddycmu/demystify-long-cot.

papers.title: FaithCoT-Bench: Benchmarking Instance-Level Faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: do these reasoning steps faithfully represent the model’s internal decision process, or are they merely surface-level accounts designed to appear aligned with the instruction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FAITHCOT-BENCH, the first comprehensive benchmark for instance-level Chain-of-Thought faithfulness detection, providing a task formulation, an expert-annotated dataset (FINE-COT), and a systematic evaluation of detection methods.
papers.conclusion: FAITHCOT-BENCH establishes the first comprehensive benchmark for instance-level CoT faithfulness, setting a solid basis for future research toward more interpretable and trustworthy reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CoT faithfulness does not align perfectly with task-level accuracy; higher accuracy does not imply more faithful reasoning.
At the instance level, correctness and faithfulness diverge; correct answers can be unfaithful, and incorrect answers can be faithful.
Faithfulness varies systematically across models; larger or more instruction-tuned models produce more faithful CoTs but still have substantial unfaithful rates.
Task type strongly influences faithfulness; knowledge-intensive tasks trigger more unfaithful reasoning than symbolic reasoning tasks.
Problem difficulty and distribution shift increase unfaithfulness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly rely on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting to improve problem-solving and provide seemingly transparent explanations. However, growing evidence shows that CoT often fail to faithfully represent the underlying reasoning process, raising concerns about their reliability in high-risk applications. Although prior studies have focused on mechanism-level analyses showing that CoTs can be unfaithful, they leave open the practical challenge of deciding whether a specific trajectory is faithful to the internal reasoning of the model. To address this gap, we introduce FaithCoT-Bench, a unified benchmark for instance-level CoT unfaithfulness detection. Our framework establishes a rigorous task formulation that formulates unfaithfulness detection as a discriminative decision problem, and provides FINE-CoT (Faithfulness instance evaluation for Chain-of-Thought), an expert-annotated collection of over 1,000 trajectories generated by four representative LLMs across four domains, including more than 300 unfaithful instances with fine-grained causes and step-level evidence. We further conduct a systematic evaluation of eleven representative detection methods spanning counterfactual, logit-based, and LLM-as-judge paradigms, deriving empirical insights that clarify the strengths and weaknesses of existing approaches and reveal the increased challenges of detection in knowledge-intensive domains and with more advanced models. To the best of our knowledge, FaithCoT-Bench establishes the first comprehensive benchmark for instance-level CoT faithfulness, setting a solid basis for future research toward more interpretable and trustworthy reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Opening the Black Box: A Survey on the Mechanisms of Multi-Step Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that enable multi-step reasoning in large language models, covering both implicit (latent) and explicit (e.g., Chain-of-Thought) reasoning paradigms?
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying multi-step reasoning in large language models, organizing existing research around seven interconnected research questions and highlighting future research directions.
papers.conclusion: The survey concludes by highlighting five open research directions for future mechanistic understanding of multi-step reasoning in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Implicit multi-hop reasoning in LLMs is an orchestrated, layered process with distinct modules specializing in different phases, but it is constrained by the fixed depth of transformers.
Implicit reasoning capability emerges via grokking, a phase transition from memorization to generalization, influenced by training data distribution, data scale, and optimization biases.
LLMs frequently bypass genuine multi-step reasoning by using shortcuts, such as direct input-output associations (factual shortcuts) or surface-level heuristics (structural shortcuts).
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting activates a 'reasoning mode' where models use generated tokens as external memory, breaking the depth limitation and enhancing computational expressiveness and generalization.
CoT does not equate to faithful explainability; it often functions as post-hoc rationalization due to a structural mismatch between the distributed, parallel computation of transformers and the sequential nature of explicit reasoning.
future_direction: Rigorous causal analysis in real-world settings
Bridging the faithfulness gap of explicit CoT reasoning
Mechanistic understanding of Latent CoT reasoning
White-box evaluation metrics for LLM reasoning
From mechanistic interpretation to model control
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities to solve problems requiring multiple reasoning steps, yet the internal mechanisms enabling such capabilities remain elusive. Unlike existing surveys that primarily focus on engineering methods to enhance performance, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the mechanisms underlying LLM multi-step reasoning. We organize the survey around a conceptual framework comprising seven interconnected research questions, from how LLMs execute implicit multi-hop reasoning within hidden activations to how verbalized explicit reasoning remodels the internal computation. Finally, we highlight five research directions for future mechanistic studies.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: Dissecting Chain-of-Thought: Compositionality through In-Context Filtering and Learning
papers.research_question: Does CoT improve in-context learning of MLPs, and what are the underlying mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: CoT breaks down in-context learning of a compositional function into two phases: filtering data related to each step and in-context learning the single-step function, which reduces sample complexity and enables learning of complex functions.
papers.conclusion: CoT decomposes in-context learning into filtering and ICL phases, providing benefits in sample complexity and approximation, and invites further investigation into its role in complex reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
CoT significantly reduces the sample complexity of in-context learning.
CoT facilitates learning of complex functions that non-CoT methods struggle with.
Transformers can implement CoT by incorporating additional layers that perform data-filtering via attention.
CoT helps accelerate pretraining by learning shortcuts to represent complex functions.
CoT-I/O requires O(max(d,k)) samples to learn a 2-layer MLP, compared to Ω(dk) for ICL.
papers.limitation:
Theoretical and empirical results are based on simple function classes (MLPs).
Analysis assumes an idealized transformer that can perfectly implement filtering and gradient descent.
Have not explored the role of CoT in more complex reasoning tasks such as natural language reasoning.
future_direction: Extending analysis to more complex function classes and real-world tasks.
Investigating the role of CoT in natural language reasoning.
Exploring the connection between CoT and other prompting techniques.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) is a method that enables language models to handle complex reasoning tasks by decomposing them into simpler steps. Despite its success, the underlying mechanics of CoT are not yet fully understood. In an attempt to shed light on this, our study investigates the impact of CoT on the ability of transformers to in-context learn a simple to study, yet general family of compositional functions: multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). In this setting, we find that the success of CoT can be attributed to breaking down in-context learning of a compositional function into two distinct phases: focusing on and filtering data related to each step of the composition and in-context learning the single-step composition function. Through both experimental and theoretical evidence, we demonstrate how CoT significantly reduces the sample complexity of in-context learning (ICL) and facilitates the learning of complex functions that non-CoT methods struggle with. Furthermore, we illustrate how transformers can transition from vanilla in-context learning to mastering a compositional function with CoT by simply incorporating additional layers that perform the necessary data-filtering for CoT via the attention mechanism. In addition to these test-time benefits, we show CoT helps accelerate pretraining by learning shortcuts to represent complex functions and filtering plays an important role in this process. These findings collectively provide insights into the mechanics of CoT, inviting further investigation of its role in complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Do All Autoregressive Transformers Remember Facts the Same Way? A Cross-Architecture Analysis of Recall Mechanisms
papers.research_question: Do findings on factual recall mechanisms in GPT-style models generalize across different autoregressive Transformer architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that factual recall mechanisms differ across autoregressive Transformer architectures, with Qwen-based models relying more on Attention modules compared to GPT-based models which use MLP modules.
papers.conclusion: Architectural variations in autoregressive Transformers lead to different mechanisms of factual recall, emphasizing the need for architecture-aware approaches in model editing and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
In GPT-based models, MLP modules in early layers play a key role in storing factual associations.
In Qwen-based models, early Attention layers contribute more to factual recall than MLP modules.
Gini coefficient analysis shows that Attention modules in Qwen models have concentrated effects on factual recall.
Semantic similarity-based evaluation confirms the differential contributions of Attention and MLP modules across architectures.
The severing effects method has limitations in accurately reflecting the contribution of Attention modules to factual recall.
papers.limitation:
the internal mechanisms by which factual associations are recalled during inference remain insufficiently understood
how factual associations are dynamically accessed across different architectures remains unclear
the interpretation of such structural differences is limited
papers.abstract: Understanding how Transformer-based language models store and retrieve factual associations is critical for improving interpretability and enabling targeted model editing. Prior work, primarily on GPT-style models, has identified MLP modules in early layers as key contributors to factual recall. However, it remains unclear whether these findings generalize across different autoregressive architectures. To address this, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of factual recall across several models -- including GPT, LLaMA, Qwen, and DeepSeek -- analyzing where and how factual information is encoded and accessed. Consequently, we find that Qwen-based models behave differently from previous patterns: attention modules in the earliest layers contribute more to factual recall than MLP modules. Our findings suggest that even within the autoregressive Transformer family, architectural variations can lead to fundamentally different mechanisms of factual recall.

papers.title: Analyzing Chain-of-Thought Prompting in Large Language Models via Gradient-based Feature Attributions
papers.research_question: What is the effect of chain-of-thought prompting on the saliency scores of input tokens in large language models, and does it make model behavior more robust to question perturbations and output variations?
papers.core_contribution: Chain-of-thought prompting does not increase the magnitude of saliency scores for semantically relevant input tokens compared to standard prompting, but it increases the robustness of these scores to question rewordings and stochasticity in model output.
papers.conclusion: Even at model scales where accuracy improvements from CoT prompting do not materialize, its use induces significant changes in saliency scores, highlighting the need for mechanistic investigation. The methodology of using gradient-based feature attribution is an effective step towards characterizing model responsiveness to CoT.
papers.key_findings:
CoT prompting does not improve model accuracy at the 6B parameter scale (except on SST), corroborating prior scale findings.
CoT prompting decreases the absolute magnitude of saliency scores for relevant input tokens across all datasets compared to standard prompting.
CoT prompting makes saliency scores more robust to question rewordings, showing less variation between original and reworded versions.
CoT prompting increases the stability of saliency scores across random model outputs, resulting in lower variance across repeated runs.
The 'dilution' of saliency scores under CoT may be due to longer prompt length and the model spreading attention over more tokens.
papers.limitation:
Limited to models of up to 6B parameters due to computational constraints, so findings may not generalize to larger models where CoT is more effective.
Small dataset size (50 questions per dataset) may limit statistical power and generalizability.
Manual annotation of relevant tokens is subjective and may introduce inconsistency.
future_direction: Repeat the methodology on larger models to examine if findings differ or become more conclusive.
Increase the number of questions and datasets evaluated for greater statistical rigor.
Use more procedural methods (e.g., spaCy) for identifying relevant tokens and crowdsourcing for generating reworded questions.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting has been shown to empirically improve the accuracy of large language models (LLMs) on various question answering tasks. While understanding why CoT prompting is effective is crucial to ensuring that this phenomenon is a consequence of desired model behavior, little work has addressed this; nonetheless, such an understanding is a critical prerequisite for responsible model deployment. We address this question by leveraging gradient-based feature attribution methods which produce saliency scores that capture the influence of input tokens on model output. Specifically, we probe several open-source LLMs to investigate whether CoT prompting affects the relative importances they assign to particular input tokens. Our results indicate that while CoT prompting does not increase the magnitude of saliency scores attributed to semantically relevant tokens in the prompt compared to standard few-shot prompting, it increases the robustness of saliency scores to question perturbations and variations in model output.

papers.title: Weight-of-Thought Reasoning: Exploring Neural Network Weights for Enhanced LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can neural network weights be examined before inference to identify and enhance reasoning pathways in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Weight-of-Thought reasoning, a novel approach that analyzes neural network weights prior to inference to identify and structure latent reasoning pathways, leading to improved performance and interpretability on complex reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: Weight-of-Thought reasoning represents a significant step toward more structured, efficient, and interpretable reasoning in neural networks by leveraging the weight space, offering a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
WoT reasoning outperforms traditional methods like Chain-of-Thought on diverse reasoning tasks, especially complex multi-step problems.
The WoT model achieves superior performance with only ~2M parameters, demonstrating high parameter efficiency compared to large LLM baselines (~175B parameters).
Ablation studies show that weight-directed guidance, graph-based message passing, node specialization, and iterative refinement are all critical components contributing to WoT's performance.
Internal analysis reveals node specialization and dynamic, task-adaptive information flow within the reasoning graph.
WoT's graph structure enables parallel processing and adaptive information routing, moving beyond sequential reasoning chains.
papers.limitation:
Generalization capability across all types of reasoning problems requires further investigation.
The all-to-all message passing mechanism scales quadratically with the number of reasoning nodes, posing potential scaling challenges.
Performance is contingent on the quality and diversity of the training data.
Integrating WoT principles directly within the architecture of extremely large, pre-existing language models presents non-trivial technical hurdles.
Evaluation primarily relies on accuracy and MSE metrics, which may not fully encompass all facets of reasoning quality.
future_direction: Investigating generalization across broader reasoning problem types.
Addressing the quadratic scaling challenge of the message passing mechanism.
Developing integration techniques for large pre-existing language models and broader evaluation metrics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning capabilities when prompted with strategies such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT).However, these approaches focus on token-level output without considering internal weight dynamics.We introduce Weight-of-Thought (WoT) reasoning, a novel approach that examines neural network weights before inference to identify reasoning pathways.Unlike existing methods, WoT explores the weight space through graph-based message passing, multi-step reasoning processes, and attention mechanisms.Our implementation creates an interconnected graph of reasoning nodes.Experiments on diverse reasoning tasks (syllogistic, mathematical, algebraic, combinatorial, and geometric) demonstrate that WoT achieves superior performance compared to traditional methods, particularly for complex problems.This approach leads to both improved performance and greater interpretability of the reasoning process, offering a promising direction for enhancing LLM reasoning capabilities.

papers.title: A Survey on Latent Reasoning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates latent reasoning as an alternative to explicit chain-of-thought in large language models, exploring its methods, benefits, and future directions.
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of latent reasoning, categorizing methods into activation-based and hidden state-based approaches, and discusses future directions for research at the frontier of LLM cognition.
papers.conclusion: The survey unifies perspectives on latent reasoning and charts future directions for research at the frontier of LLM cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Latent reasoning performs multi-step inference in continuous hidden states, offering higher bandwidth than explicit chain-of-thought.
Activation-based methods create deeper computational graphs by iteratively processing information through the same layers.
Hidden-state-based methods expand temporal capacity by evolving hidden states over sequences.
Diffusion models enable infinite-depth reasoning through bidirectional context and iterative refinement.
Layer specialization theory suggests different layers play distinct roles in latent reasoning, analogous to steps in explicit CoT.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities, especially when guided by explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning that verbalizes intermediate steps. While CoT improves both interpretability and accuracy, its dependence on natural language reasoning limits the model's expressive bandwidth. Latent reasoning tackles this bottleneck by performing multi-step inference entirely in the model's continuous hidden state, eliminating token-level supervision. To advance latent reasoning research, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the emerging field of latent reasoning. We begin by examining the foundational role of neural network layers as the computational substrate for reasoning, highlighting how hierarchical representations support complex transformations. Next, we explore diverse latent reasoning methodologies, including activation-based recurrence, hidden state propagation, and fine-tuning strategies that compress or internalize explicit reasoning traces. Finally, we discuss advanced paradigms such as infinite-depth latent reasoning via masked diffusion models, which enable globally consistent and reversible reasoning processes. By unifying these perspectives, we aim to clarify the conceptual landscape of latent reasoning and chart future directions for research at the frontier of LLM cognition. An associated GitHub repository collecting the latest papers and repos is available at: https://github.com/multimodal-art-projection/LatentCoT-Horizon/.

papers.title: Demystifying Reasoning Dynamics with Mutual Information: Thinking Tokens are Information Peaks in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What are the critical reasoning steps or intermediate states that significantly affect the final results in the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that during the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs), certain steps exhibit sudden increases in mutual information (MI) with the correct answer, and these MI peaks correspond to 'thinking tokens' (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait') that are critical for reasoning performance. Based on this, the paper proposes two training-free methods to improve reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that thinking tokens, which correspond to MI peaks, are crucial for LRM reasoning and that leveraging these tokens can improve reasoning performance without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
During LRM reasoning, certain steps show sudden and significant increases in mutual information (MI) with the golden answer, termed MI peaks.
The tokens at MI peaks are often reflective or transitional words (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait', 'So') and are critical for reasoning performance; suppressing them significantly harms performance.
Theoretically, higher cumulative MI between representations and the golden answer leads to tighter bounds on prediction error.
Non-reasoning LLMs do not exhibit clear MI peaks, suggesting the phenomenon is a result of reasoning-intensive training.
Two proposed methods, Representation Recycling (RR) and Thinking Token based Test-time Scaling (TTTS), which leverage thinking tokens, can improve reasoning performance on math benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in complex problem-solving, yet their internal reasoning mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the reasoning trajectories of LRMs from an information-theoretic perspective. By tracking how mutual information (MI) between intermediate representations and the correct answer evolves during LRM reasoning, we observe an interesting MI peaks phenomenon: the MI at specific generative steps exhibits a sudden and significant increase during LRM's reasoning process. We theoretically analyze such phenomenon and show that as MI increases, the probability of model's prediction error decreases. Furthermore, these MI peaks often correspond to tokens expressing reflection or transition, such as ``Hmm'', ``Wait'' and ``Therefore,'' which we term as the thinking tokens. We then demonstrate that these thinking tokens are crucial for LRM's reasoning performance, while other tokens has minimal impacts. Building on these analyses, we propose two simple yet effective methods to improve LRM's reasoning performance, by delicately leveraging these thinking tokens. Overall, our work provides novel insights into the reasoning mechanisms of LRMs and offers practical ways to improve their reasoning capabilities. The code is available at https://github.com/ChnQ/MI-Peaks.

papers.title: Modeling Hierarchical Thinking in Large Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: How can we model and analyze the hierarchical reasoning dynamics of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) using a Finite State Machine (FSM) framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Finite State Machine (FSM) framework to model and analyze the hierarchical reasoning dynamics of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), providing a structured, interpretable abstraction for comparing reasoning behaviors.
papers.conclusion: The FSM formalization provides a structured, interpretable lens for visualizing reasoning as trajectories in state space, revealing how models explore, refine, and converge on solutions, and offers a model-agnostic foundation for comparing reasoning behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Longer FSM traces correlate strongly with higher accuracy on structured mathematical problems, but this correlation weakens for open-domain factual knowledge tasks where longer reasoning can introduce redundancy.
High-performing models often combine consistent deduction with periods of uncertainty assessment and occasional backtracking, while weaker models tend to explore less and finish early.
Effective reasoning emerges not merely from FSM length but from adaptive state regulation that supports iterative refinement and stable convergence.
Mathematical reasoning is goal-directed: strong models try different exploration strategies through augmentation and uncertainty-estimation, then refine their steps with deduction and backtracking to reach a precise solution.
Scientific knowledge reasoning is evidence-driven: strong models build their answers step by step, combining augmentation and deduction with active use of uncertainty-estimation to adjust and revise their intermediate beliefs.
papers.limitation:
The FSM representation discretizes continuous, context-dependent reasoning into symbolic states, potentially overlooking subtle or overlapping cognitive transitions.
The annotation process relies on LLM-based labeling, which may introduce segmentation noise or bias in assigning state boundaries.
The fixed taxonomy of six reasoning states may not fully generalize to multimodal reasoning or interactive dialogue contexts.
The framework focuses on reasoning behavior rather than correctness; FSM metrics describe process dynamics but do not directly measure factual or logical accuracy.
future_direction: Exploring automatic or adaptive state discovery
Cross-domain calibration and human-aligned validation to refine interpretability and robustness
Exploring richer models (e.g., pushdown automata) for more accurate representations of reasoning progression
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning abilities when they generate step-by-step solutions, known as chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. When trained to using chain-of-thought reasoning examples, the resulting models (called Large Reasoning Models, or LRMs) appear to learn hierarchical thinking strategies similar to those used by humans. However, understanding LRMs emerging reasoning capabilities remains a difficult open problem, with many potential important applications including improving training and understanding robustness. In this paper, we adopt a memoryless Finite State Machine formulation to approximate LRM's emerging hierarchical reasoning dynamics as a structured, interpretable abstraction. We identify a small set of discrete reasoning states including - initialization, deduction, augmentation-strategy, uncertainty-estimation, backtracking, and final-conclusion that capture the high-level states present in the model's reasoning process. By annotating each step of a model's CoT with these states, we can represent the reasoning trajectory as a transition sequence through the state graph. This FSM formulation provides a systematic way to analyze, interpret and visualize how different models approach problems. We describe the FSM model, provide examples of CoT annotations under this scheme, and discuss how it can shed light on differences between available models in their approach to reasoning. Our results demonstrate that this FSM-based analysis reveals distinct reasoning patterns and potential shortcomings, offering a new lens to evaluate and improve LLM reasoning.

papers.title: How Does Unfaithful Reasoning Emerge from Autoregressive Training? A Study of Synthetic Experiments
papers.research_question: What constitutes faithful chain-of-thought reasoning and how does unfaithfulness emerge from autoregressive training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic task (AER) to study chain-of-thought faithfulness, finds a critical noise threshold for faithful reasoning due to simplicity bias, and identifies training phases with emergent self-verification.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that unfaithful reasoning emerges when noise exceeds a critical threshold, driven by simplicity bias, and that models develop implicit self-verification through training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Faithful reasoning is possible only when training noise is below a critical threshold.
Simplicity bias explains the threshold: models prefer simpler stepwise reasoning over skip-step reasoning.
Training dynamics exhibit three reasoning modes: stepwise, mixed, skip-step, with a transient increase in prediction entropy in the mixed mode.
Models learn to encode internal uncertainty, suggesting emergent implicit self-verification.
Shortcut features amplify unfaithfulness.
papers.limitation:
Focus on autoregressive training, not reinforcement learning with verifier rewards.
Potential over-generalization of findings beyond the synthetic task.
future_direction: Investigate reinforcement learning with verifier rewards (RLVR).
Apply metrics to LLMs beyond synthetic setting.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning generated by large language models (LLMs) is often unfaithful: intermediate steps can be logically inconsistent or fail to reflect the causal relationship leading to the final answer. Despite extensive empirical observations, a fundamental understanding of CoT is lacking--what constitutes faithful CoT reasoning, and how unfaithfulness emerges from autoregressive training. We study these questions using well-controlled synthetic experiments, training small transformers on noisy data to solve modular arithmetic expressions step by step, a task we term Arithmetic Expression Reasoning. We find that models can learn faithful reasoning that causally follows the underlying arithmetic rules, but only when the training noise is below a critical threshold, a phenomenon attributable to simplicity bias. At higher noise levels, training dynamics exhibit a transition from faithful stepwise reasoning to unfaithful skip-step reasoning via an intermediate mixed mode characterized by a transient increase in prediction entropy. Mechanistic analysis reveals that models learn to encode internal uncertainty by resolving inconsistent reasoning steps, which suggests the emergence of implicit self-verification from autoregressive training.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether and how existing transformer large language models can solve compositional relational reasoning tasks.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark to evaluate compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency and identifying core circuits and True/False heads that play key roles.
papers.conclusion: Proposes the GAR benchmark that is challenging for LLMs and simple enough for MI study, shows compositionality gap increases with scaling, and discovers circuits including True/False heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.key_findings:
GAR benchmark is challenging for existing LLMs, with GPT-4 achieving only 71.5% accuracy.
Compositionality gap increases with model scaling, indicating fundamental deficiency in CRR.
Core circuits are discovered in Vicuna-33B, including truthfulness and ICL sub-circuits.
True and False heads are identified, representing abstract notions of true and false in GAR tasks.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts performance.
papers.limitation: Do not use automatic circuit discovery methods due to model size and circuit complexity
future_direction: Developing automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play a fundamental role in CRR across various models and tasks. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/Caiyun-AI/GAR.

papers.title: Diagnosing Pathological Chain-of-Thought in Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is fundamental to modern LLM architectures and represents a critical intervention point for AI safety. However, CoT reasoning may exhibit failure modes that we note as pathologies, which prevent it from being useful for monitoring. Prior work has identified three distinct pathologies: post-hoc rationalization, where models generate plausible explanations backwards from predetermined answers; encoded reasoning, where intermediate steps conceal information within seemingly interpretable text; and internalized reasoning, where models replace explicit reasoning with meaningless filler tokens while computing internally. To better understand and discriminate between these pathologies, we create a set of concrete metrics that are simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, and task-agnostic. To validate our approach, we develop model organisms deliberately trained to exhibit specific CoT pathologies. Our work provides a practical toolkit for assessing CoT pathologies, with direct implications for training-time monitoring.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Tokens are Computer Program Variables
papers.research_question: What is the role of CoT tokens in LLMs for compositional reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: CoT tokens function like variables in computer programs, storing intermediate values that are used in subsequent computations and are causally related to the final output.
papers.conclusion: CoT tokens behave like variables in computer programs, storing intermediate values that are causally connected to the output, but models may learn shortcuts and there is a computational complexity limit.
papers.key_findings:
CoT is essential for solving compositional problems like multi-digit multiplication and dynamic programming.
Removing non-result tokens (keeping only intermediate results) does not harm performance, indicating that intermediate results are the key.
Intermediate results can be stored in different forms (e.g., latent tokens) without performance drop, unless compression exceeds a complexity limit.
Intervening on CoT token values changes subsequent reasoning and final output, showing causal relation.
Models sometimes take shortcuts in easy subproblems, making interventions fail.
papers.limitation:
No theoretical proof is provided for the hypothesis that CoT tokens function like variables.
Experiments are conducted on two synthetic tasks with one model (Qwen-2.5-1.5B), and not on real-world datasets.
future_direction: Generalization ability of CoT programs.
Identification of intermediate variable tokens in general tasks.
Estimation of computational complexity between variable tokens.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thoughts (CoT) requires large language models (LLMs) to generate intermediate steps before reaching the final answer, and has been proven effective to help LLMs solve complex reasoning tasks. However, the inner mechanism of CoT still remains largely unclear. In this paper, we empirically study the role of CoT tokens in LLMs on two compositional tasks: multi-digit multiplication and dynamic programming. While CoT is essential for solving these problems, we find that preserving only tokens that store intermediate results would achieve comparable performance. Furthermore, we observe that storing intermediate results in an alternative latent form will not affect model performance. We also randomly intervene some values in CoT, and notice that subsequent CoT tokens and the final answer would change correspondingly. These findings suggest that CoT tokens may function like variables in computer programs but with potential drawbacks like unintended shortcuts and computational complexity limits between tokens. The code and data are available at https://github.com/solitaryzero/CoTs_are_Variables.

papers.title: Calibrating Reasoning in Language Models with Internal Consistency
papers.research_question: How can internal representations in large language models be used to calibrate reasoning, specifically by measuring inconsistencies between intermediate and final layers during chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes internal consistency as a novel measure to evaluate LLM confidence in reasoning by examining agreement of latent predictions from intermediate layers, and shows that up-weighting paths with high internal consistency significantly boosts reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Internal consistency is a robust indicator of correct reasoning paths and can be leveraged to enhance the reliability of reasoning in LLMs through calibration.
papers.key_findings:
CoT reasoning leads to inconsistencies between middle and final layer representations, indicating uncertainty.
Internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths.
Up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency improves reasoning accuracy across various tasks.
Patterns in attention and feed-forward networks across layers provide insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency.
Layer-weighted aggregation of internal consistency finds transferable patterns that generalize across tasks.
papers.limitation:
The study is restricted to decoder-only models.
The analysis focuses on vanilla chain-of-thought prompting, not other complex prompting techniques.
future_direction: Extending the concept of internal consistency to encoder-decoder models.
Investigating internal consistency under more complex prompting scenarios.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in various reasoning tasks, aided by techniques like chain-of-thought prompting that elicits verbalized reasoning. However, LLMs often generate text with obvious mistakes and contradictions, raising doubts about their ability to robustly process and utilize generated rationales. In this work, we investigate reasoning in LLMs through the lens of internal representations, focusing on how these representations are influenced by generated rationales. Our preliminary analysis reveals that while generated rationales improve answer accuracy, inconsistencies emerge between the model's internal representations in middle layers and those in final layers, potentially undermining the reliability of their reasoning processes. To address this, we propose internal consistency as a measure of the model's confidence by examining the agreement of latent predictions decoded from intermediate layers. Extensive empirical studies across different models and datasets demonstrate that internal consistency effectively distinguishes between correct and incorrect reasoning paths. Motivated by this, we propose a new approach to calibrate reasoning by up-weighting reasoning paths with high internal consistency, resulting in a significant boost in reasoning performance. Further analysis uncovers distinct patterns in attention and feed-forward modules across layers, providing insights into the emergence of internal inconsistency. In summary, our results demonstrate the potential of using internal representations for self-evaluation of LLMs. Our code is available at github.com/zhxieml/internal-consistency.

papers.title: Activation Control for Efficiently Eliciting Long Chain-of-thought Ability of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can the long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning ability in large language models be efficiently elicited by understanding and controlling internal activation mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a training-free activation control method (EELo-CoT) that elicits long chain-of-thought reasoning by amplifying key MLP activations and inserting 'wait' tokens, and a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a small amplification module and LoRA layers.
papers.conclusion: By identifying and controlling a small set of key activations, the long chain-of-thought ability can be efficiently elicited in LLMs, leading to improved reasoning performance and self-reflection.
papers.key_findings:
Long-CoT related activations are sparse and primarily located in the last few layers of the model.
Amplifying these key activations and inserting 'wait' tokens can induce long CoT reasoning, increasing self-reflection rate and accuracy.
Activation changes around trigger tokens follow predictable patterns (sharp rise then logarithmic decay).
The proposed training-free EELo-CoT method improves accuracy and self-reflection on math and science reasoning benchmarks.
A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method, training only 1.51% of parameters, outperforms LoRA and matches full fine-tuning on some benchmarks.
papers.limitation:
The activation intervention rules are simple and may not capture nuanced activation patterns that require more sophisticated stimulation.
Experiments are limited to models up to 32B parameters and do not extend to ultra-large or mixture-of-experts architectures.
The focus on self-reflection does not disentangle other latent capabilities that may be triggered by long CoT, such as elaboration without verification or memorization.
future_direction: Apply the method to multimodal LLMs (e.g., VLM and Video-LLM).
Test the method on more complex planning tasks (e.g., visual reasoning and GUI operation).
Test the generalizability of the method to non-transformer architectures (e.g., Mamba).
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable reasoning performance, eliciting the long chain-of-thought (CoT) ability in large language models (LLMs) typically requires costly reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning on high-quality distilled data. We investigate the internal mechanisms behind this capability and show that a small set of high-impact activations in the last few layers largely governs long-form reasoning attributes, such as output length and self-reflection. By simply amplifying these activations and inserting "wait" tokens, we can invoke the long CoT ability without any training, resulting in significantly increased self-reflection rates and accuracy. Moreover, we find that the activation dynamics follow predictable trajectories, with a sharp rise after special tokens and a subsequent exponential decay. Building on these insights, we introduce a general training-free activation control technique. It leverages a few contrastive examples to identify key activations, and employs simple analytic functions to modulate their values at inference time to elicit long CoTs. Extensive experiments confirm the effectiveness of our method in efficiently eliciting long CoT reasoning in LLMs and improving their performance. Additionally, we propose a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains only a last-layer activation amplification module and a few LoRA layers, outperforming full LoRA fine-tuning on reasoning benchmarks with significantly fewer parameters. Our code and data are publicly released.

papers.title: Meaningless Tokens, Meaningful Gains: How Activation Shifts Enhance LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: Why does inserting meaningless tokens improve LLM reasoning performance, and how can this effect be harnessed?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic explanation for how meaningless tokens improve LLM reasoning via activation redistribution and introduces ARM, a lightweight inference-time method that reproduces this effect.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that activation redistribution is a key mechanism behind the meaningless-token effect and that ARM effectively harnesses this mechanism to improve LLM reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Inserting meaningless tokens induces an affine transformation on attention outputs, leading to activation redistribution in MLP layers.
Activation redistribution reduces near-zero activations and increases variance, enhancing the model's representational capacity for reasoning.
The proposed ARM method adaptively shifts near-zero activations outward, improving reasoning performance without changing input tokens.
ARM consistently improves performance across diverse models and reasoning benchmarks while being simple to implement.
papers.limitation:
Our method is primarily evaluated on reasoning tasks; its effectiveness on non-reasoning tasks is limited.
The hyperparameters of ARM need to be tuned per model family.
future_direction: Extending ARM to more layers or combining it with other inference-time optimizations.
Exploring the effect on non-reasoning tasks and automatic hyperparameter tuning.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the puzzling observation that inserting long sequences of meaningless tokens before the query prompt can consistently enhance LLM reasoning performance, this work analyzes the underlying mechanism driving this phenomenon and based on these insights proposes a more principled method that allows for similar performance gains. First, we find that the improvements arise from a redistribution of activations in the LLM's MLP layers, where near zero activations become less frequent while large magnitude activations increase. This redistribution enhances the model's representational capacity by suppressing weak signals and promoting stronger, more informative ones. Building on this insight, we propose the Activation Redistribution Module (ARM), a lightweight inference-time technique that modifies activations directly without altering the input sequence. ARM adaptively identifies near-zero activations after the non-linear function and shifts them outward, implicitly reproducing the beneficial effects of meaningless tokens in a controlled manner. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and model architectures clearly show that ARM consistently improves LLM performance on reasoning tasks while requiring only a few lines of simple code to implement. Our findings deliver both a clear mechanistic explanation for the unexpected benefits of meaningless tokens and a simple yet effective technique that harnesses activation redistribution to further improve LLM performance.

papers.title: Pierce the Mists, Greet the Sky: Decipher Knowledge Overshadowing via Knowledge Circuit Analysis
papers.research_question: What are the origins and internal mechanisms of knowledge overshadowing (a type of hallucination) during model training, and how can it be analyzed and mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PHANTOM CIRCUIT, a framework that uses knowledge circuit analysis to comprehensively analyze the training dynamics and internal mechanisms of knowledge overshadowing, a specific type of hallucination in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: PHANTOM CIRCUIT provides a mechanistic understanding of knowledge overshadowing, tracing its evolution during training and revealing internal circuit mechanisms, offering a new methodological lens for its analysis and potential mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Higher knowledge popularity (P) and model size (M) lead to earlier onset, shorter duration, and quicker recovery from overshadowing, while larger dataset size (D) leads to earlier onset but slower recovery.
The dynamic nature of overshadowing arises from the co-evolution between the loss proportion of subordinate knowledge (LP) and the overshadowing rate (RO); insufficient optimization of subordinate knowledge leads to overshadowing.
The knowledge circuit's attentional allocation to the differences between dominant and subordinate knowledge influences the extent of overshadowing; high-attention heads are crucial for recovery.
Knowledge circuit-guided optimization (pruning edges to an optimal circuit) is a promising strategy to mitigate the overshadowing effect.
papers.limitation:
The conclusions are based on controlled experiments with synthetic data and specific model architectures (Pythia, GPT-2). Generalization to other architectures and complex, noisy real-world data remains to be validated.
The applicability to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation remains a key area for future exploration.
Performing dynamic analysis of knowledge circuits throughout the entire training process is computationally intensive, potentially hindering scalability to very large models or extensive training runs.
future_direction: Validate the conclusions on other model architectures and more complex, noisy real-world data.
Explore the applicability of PHANTOM CIRCUIT to practical tasks like multi-hop reasoning and code generation.
Develop more computationally efficient circuit extraction techniques to improve scalability.
